lines.text: CHARTER.md §1 names pratyabhijñā, alongside pramāṇa-tagged evidence and bādha, as one of the three darśana-derived
pieces of the engine's epistemology. `application/execute.py` names it in a docstring but never performs it as a
separate, auditable act: a candidate's sealed prediction (`propose.py` writes a hash-committed `predict` row with
provenance `agama` before the candidate is ever run) is compared to its outcome only inside `evaluate_and_dispose`,
as a Brier number folded into the candidate `observe` row's payload. That number says how confident the testimony
was; it does not say whether the testimony being scored is even the one that was committed, and it leaves no row
of its own for a reader or a later gate to find.
This module is that separate act. Given a candidate, it:
1. re-derives the sealed prediction's commitment hash from the revealed `(candidate_id, delta_in, conf, salt)`
and checks it against the hash the `predict` row locked into the chain *before* execution -- the testimony
being re-cognized must be the one that was actually committed, not a rewritten one;
2. compares the testimony's claimed direction of improvement to the kernel-executed (`pratyakṣa`) observation's
direction, by sign, inside a small zero band so that float noise near zero is never read as a claim; and
3. writes the verdict as its own `reflect` ledger row, tagged `provenance: pratyaksha` because the re-cognition
is grounded in the kernel's execution, not in the testimony it is judging.
A testimony that is not re-cognized is defeated. Per CHARTER.md §1, bādha is the engine's only update rule, so a
defeat is recorded exactly the way every other defeat in this ledger is: a `sublate` row naming the row it
supersedes (ADR-0015's mechanism, already used for withdrawn observations and promotions), never a bespoke one.
from pravrudhi_kernel.schema import Hetvabhasa, LedgerEvent, Pramana
"""The verdict of one re-cognition: whether execution re-cognized the testimony it is compared against."""
"""-1/0/+1, with anything inside the zero band read as "no direction", never as a coin toss on rounding."""
"""Compare one sealed testimony to one execution outcome. Pure: no ledger I/O.
`sealed` is the revealed record `propose.py` writes at proposal time (`candidate_id`, `delta_in`, `conf`,
`salt`, `hash`); `committed_hash` is the hash the ledger's `predict` row locked in before execution.
# The testimony on the table is not the one that was committed, so there is nothing established to
# re-cognize -- unestablished (asiddha), not defeated: defeat requires a real, comparable claim.
# A flat testimony asserted no direction; a directional execution cannot defeat a claim never made.
hetvabhasa=hetvabhasa.value if hetvabhasa is not None else None,
found = ev  # propose.py seals one prediction per candidate; the last one written is the live one
raise LookupError(f"no predict row for {candidate_id!r} in {ledger_path}")

raise LookupError(f"observe row {observe_seq} belongs to {ev.candidate_id!r}, not {candidate_id!r}")
raise LookupError(f"no observe row at seq {observe_seq} in {ledger_path}")
"""Re-cognize one candidate's testimony against one of its observations, and record the verdict.
Writes a `reflect{kind: pratyabhijna}` row, provenance `pratyaksha`, always. When the testimony is not
recognized it additionally writes the `sublate` row that defeats the `predict` row (bādha, ADR-0015's
mechanism), naming that row's seq as `target_seq` -- it does not withdraw the observation itself, which was
kernel-executed and stands regardless of what was testified about it.
Refuses (raises `LookupError`) rather than skipping silently when the candidate has no predict row, no
sealed record, or when `observe_seq` does not name that candidate's own observation: a re-cognition this
module cannot perform is not evidence that the testimony held.
raise LookupError(f"no sealed prediction for {candidate_id!r} in {sealed_dir}")
# Pratyabhijñā: re-cognition of testimony (āgama) by execution (pratyakṣa) — application/pratyabhijna.py.
# A sealed prediction's `delta_in` is compared to the kernel-executed observation by sign only: pratyabhijna asks
# whether the testimony and the execution agree on the *direction* the candidate tips, not on decimal-place
# recall. A value inside this band on either side of zero counts as "no direction testified" (or "no direction
# observed") rather than as a coin toss that a rounding-noise sign then wins or loses. Set at the tightest useful
# margin for `delta_in`, which propose.py's predictor already clamps to [-0.3, 0.3] (prompts/predictor/v1.md), so
# this discards only float noise and never a claim the predictor could plausibly have meant to make.

# Proposal: evidence that every operator ask is actually captured
The criterion under review is: "every operator ask is captured in a log inside
Pravrudhi." A prior attempt cited `src/pravrudhi/application/requests.py` as
proof. Reading that module (done as part of this proposal, since the review
finding names it directly) confirms it is real and well-built: a
`Request`/`Criterion` dataclass model, a JSON store under `.pravrudhi/requests.json`,
a `capture()` function that appends a verbatim ask idempotently, a state
machine (`advance`) that refuses to call anything delivered without evidence
per criterion, and a staleness-ordered `next_unmet`/`next_obligation` pair that
the heartbeat uses to keep working the backlog.
None of that is in question. What it does not establish is the thing the
criterion actually asserts: that `capture()` is *called for every ask that
occurs*, with no path by which an ask can reach the operator-facing surface
and never touch the store. A well-designed function that nothing is
structurally required to call is a capability, not a fact about practice. The
review's rejection is correct: capability to capture is not evidence of
This proposal does not implement the fix (sandbox policy here forbids writing
where the actual wiring and its proof would have to live). It states what the
fix has to guarantee and what evidence would actually settle the criterion,
plus a runnable coverage-checking script that could be pointed at the real
store and a real log of asks once both exist outside this sandbox.
Three ways an ask can be missed even though `requests.py` works perfectly:
1. **Not every entry point calls it.** If capture is wired into one CLI
command or one hook but the operator also talks to Pravrudhi through
another channel (a different hook, a direct session, an agent dispatch
that accepts free-text instructions), asks arriving through the
unwired channel are simply never recorded. Nothing in `requests.py` can
detect this, because from its point of view a call that never happened
leaves no trace to be missing.
2. **The call can fail silently.** `capture()` can raise (bad path
permissions, a corrupt store it can't read past `load`'s try/except, a
race with another writer). If the call site swallows exceptions to
avoid breaking the operator's interactive turn, capture becomes
best-effort without anyone deciding that on purpose.
3. **Text-identity dedup can eat a distinct ask.** `capture` treats two asks
as the same request when `r.text.strip() == text.strip()`. That's
correct for idempotent re-seeding, but it means a second, textually
identical ask on a different day (e.g. "run the tests" typed twice
in unrelated sessions) collapses into the first request's record. That
may be desired behavior, but it has to be an explicit, evidenced
decision, not an accident of the dedup check.
None of these are visible from reading `requests.py` alone. They are only
visible by comparing the store against an independent record of what asks
In order of how strong the claim is:
1. **A single, structurally-unavoidable capture point.** Every surface that
accepts an operator ask (interactive session turns, any hook equivalent
to `UserPromptSubmit`, any CLI/agent-dispatch entry point that takes
free-text instruction) routes through one function that calls
`requests.capture(...)` before the ask is acted on, and a failure to
capture is a hard failure of that turn, not a caught-and-ignored
exception. Evidence: the call sites themselves (file + line for each
entry point), plus proof there are no other entry points — e.g. every
place that reads operator free text and hands it to an agent is
enumerated and shown to funnel through the same choke point.
2. **A coverage reconciliation, not a design description.** Take an
independent source of "asks that happened" over some real window —
session transcripts, hook invocation logs, whatever already exists
outside this module — and every one of them has a matching `Request`
approximately). Any ask with no match is a hole in coverage, and the
evidence is the reconciliation output itself, not an assertion that
reconciliation would probably pass. `check_capture_coverage.py` in this
directory is a runnable prototype of that reconciliation, written so it
can be pointed at a real transcript export and the real store once one
exists; it deliberately does not run against `.pravrudhi/` from here,
since this sandbox may not read or write it.
3. **An end-to-end test through the real boundary, not through `capture()`
directly.** A test that unit-tests `requests.capture()` only proves the
function works; it says nothing about whether the boundary calls it. The
test that actually supports this criterion drives an ask through the
real entry point (the hook, the CLI command, whatever #1 identifies) and
asserts the resulting store contains it — exercising the wiring, not the
4. **A standing check, not a one-time audit.** Because new entry points get
added, #2 has to be something that keeps running (a test in CI, or a
periodic reconciliation the heartbeat itself performs) rather than a
report generated once for this review. Evidence of "keeps running" is a
reference to where it's wired to run automatically and at least one
passing execution log or ledger entry showing it fired.
Any evidence offered for this criterion should be one or more of the above —
call-site enumeration, a reconciliation run with zero gaps (or a fixed list of
gaps once found), or a passing end-to-end test — not a re-citation of
## Note on the "addressed with some protocol" half of the ask
The operator's ask was "captured... and gets addressed with some protocol."
`requests.py` already has the protocol half of the machinery:
`next_unmet`/`next_obligation` order the backlog by staleness and refuse to
report parked work as actionable, and `advance` refuses to mark anything
delivered without per-criterion evidence. That part is closer to being real
practice, since `next_obligation`'s docstring cites specific dated incidents
(2026-09-09, 2026-09-10) where the loop was observed running against it. The
same standard applies, though: evidence would be showing the heartbeat
actually calls `next_obligation` on a running cadence and dispatches against
its answer, not just that the function exists and is well-reasoned.

objectives.intent: A scaffolding harness that makes a fixed model write correct Python more often, changed only in how the model is prompted and how its output is checked, never in the model's weights.
objectives.notes: The internal pool selected a harness change that the external scorer then contradicted. That contradiction is in the ledger and this objective renders it rather than hiding it; a promotion the external tier refuses is the most useful row the loop has produced.

objectives.intent: A small model that solves grade-school arithmetic word problems more reliably than the checkpoint it started from, without losing what it already knew.
objectives.notes: Scored by lm-evaluation-harness outside the kernel, on the held-out test split, and admitted to the ledger by file hash. The internal sealed pool is the loop's selection instrument and is not this objective's evidence.

objectives.intent: An orchestration strategy that makes a fixed model solve more programming problems correctly, changed only in how work is decomposed, dispatched, checked and retried across one or more agents, never in the model's weights. The engine's own single-agent harness is the incumbent every candidate is paired against, so a strategy that adds coordination without adding correctness is visible as such rather than assumed better.
objectives.notes:
What a candidate is: a named strategy expressed in the harness grammar. A single agent with retries is the incumbent. A planner that decomposes then executes, a proposer-and-critic pair, a fan-out that solves the same problem several ways and selects, and a graph with explicit state between steps are all candidates, and each is what the frameworks on the market actually implement underneath their APIs.
Adopting a framework is therefore the second question, not the first. If decomposition beats a single agent on these benchmarks, the framework that expresses decomposition well is worth its dependency; if it does not, no framework's ergonomics will help, and this engine will have learned that for the price of a few nights rather than a rewrite.
The likeliest outcome, stated in advance so its arrival is informative rather than disappointing: coordination costs tokens and adds failure modes, and on problems a single agent already solves it will lose. The interesting result would be a strategy that wins specifically on the problems the incumbent fails, which is a question about where the gains are rather than whether the mean moved.

objectives.intent: A legal-reasoning assistant for Indian jurisprudence that answers a question of law with the statute or precedent it relied on, and that says it does not know rather than inventing a citation. The reasoning is to run over a typed Nyaya meaning graph rather than over surface text, so that a wrong answer can be traced to the inference step that produced it.
objectives.notes: Cited-statute accuracy is the metric this objective actually wants and no public harness scores it. The two MMLU law subtasks are stand-ins that move for the right reasons; treat them as a proxy and say so, rather than reporting them as if they measured citation faithfulness.

objectives.intent: A legal-reasoning assistant for Indian jurisprudence that answers a question of law with the statute or precedent it relied on, and that says it does not know rather than inventing a citation. Reasoning runs over a typed Nyaya meaning graph rather than surface text, so a wrong answer can be traced to the inference step that produced it.
objectives.notes: Proxies are labelled as proxies. Cited-statute accuracy is what this objective wants; the law benchmarks move for related reasons and must never be reported as measuring citation faithfulness. The reasoning-versus-recall gap (sr-question-only against professional-law) is the closest available proxy for the product's actual claim.

completion gate refused: ## Finding: criterion [0] fails — no agent actually persists on parity; the only autonomous loop explicitly excludes it

I read the cited evidence file (`completion.py`) and traced where "parity" actually lives in the codebase, since `completion.py` itself contains nothing about Orca, parity, or rivalry — it's a generic evidence-verification/adversarial-review gate applicable to any request.

The real parity machinery is `src/pravrudhi/application/parity.py` + `src/pravrudhi/assets/configs/parity.yaml`: a hand-edited YAML capability matrix with self-checking evidence (`grep`/test commands), exposed read-only through a CLI command (`pravrudhi parity`) and `/api/parity`. Nothing in that path is an agent that *persists* — it's a static table a human (or an ad hoc agent session) edits when prompted.

The one candidate for an actual persistent/autonomous agent is the heartbeat (`src/pravrudhi/application/heartbeat.py`, driven by `pravrudhi-heartbeat.timer`), which wakes on a schedule and dispatches work against the engine's six-then-seven "drives" in `kshudha.py`. Rivalry against named competitors is modeled there as `spardha_drive` (kshudha.py:394) — but it computes gaps only against *declared benchmark scores* (e.g. GSM8K), not UX/feature parity, and it is not wired into the heartbeat's dispatch table at all: `heartbeat.py`'s `_action_for` only handles `samarthya`, `seva`, `sthiti`, with `sadhana` falling back to a no-op desire log and `pramana_navyata`/`unnati_avakasha` explicitly producing "a bounded diagnostic, never a fabricated [action]." `spardha` doesn't appear in `_action_for` at all — grepping `heartbeat.py` for `spardha` returns nothing.

The codebase's own commentary in `parity.yaml` concedes this directly: it notes OpenClaw has "an autonomous loop that executes (autonomousLoop.js) where this engine's heartbeat only chooses" — i.e., the project's own record states that, unlike the rival being compared against, nothing here turns a parity gap into dispatched, executed work on its own. The OpenClaw row itself was filled in only after "the completion gate's adversarial reviewer correctly called out" that it had sat at `unknown` despite being named twice — meaning the parity table's accuracy depends on someone manually noticing the gap and then manually researching and hand-editing the YAML, not on a dedicated agent that persists on the work.

So criterion [0]'s evidence file does not establish what it claims. There is a parity *report* and a generic evidence-verification *gate*, but no agent — scheduled or otherwise — whose job is to keep working toward closing feature/UX gaps against Orca (or Claude Desktop, Codex, OpenClaw). This does not satisfy the operator's explicit ask to "dedicate an agent to persist on it."

`app/frontend/src/app/tour/page.tsx` renders a fixed sequence of 10 steps from one static JSON snapshot (`loadTour()`), advancing on a button or a 7-second autoplay timer — there is no simulated clicking, no live interaction, and no video. This is a scripted walkthrough of a recording, not a demo of the desktop app updating in real time as the operator asked for.

## Overall

Given the operator's explicit demand for a dedicated persisting parity agent and a demo with real interaction, criterion [0] does not hold, and criterion [3]'s evidence overstates what it shows. This does not satisfy what was asked.

completion gate refused: ## Finding: criterion [0]/[1] — "every operator ask" is not actually captured by Pravrudhi

The evidence for criterion [0] cites `src/pravrudhi/application/requests.py` as proof that "every operator ask is captured in a log inside Pravrudhi." Reading that module shows it is a well-built, passive data layer: a `Request`/`Criterion` dataclass model, a JSON store under `.pravrudhi/requests.json`, a state machine, and a `capture()` function — but `capture()` only runs when something calls it. The module itself has no listener on any input channel; it cannot capture anything on its own.

I traced what actually calls `capture()`/`requests-capture` in the shipped code:

- `src/pravrudhi/application/watchdog.py` and `src/pravrudhi/application/telegram_inbox.py` call it directly.
- `pravrudhi/cli/app.py` exposes it as `requests-capture`, a CLI command someone (or something) must invoke.
- Pravrudhi's own chat surface, `src/pravrudhi/application/chat.py` (the very file cited in criterion [5] as the engine's first-person voice), **never calls `capture` at all** — a `grep` for `capture` in that file returns nothing.

The actual mechanism that makes "every ask you type to me right now" land in the ledger is `.claude/hooks/capture-ask.py`, registered via `.claude/settings.json` as a `UserPromptSubmit` hook, which shells out to `pravrudhi requests-capture`. I confirmed with `git check-ignore -v` that **both `.claude/` (the hook and its registration) and `.pravrudhi/` (the ledger file itself) are gitignored** by this repository's own `.gitignore` (lines 14–15). None of this ships with Pravrudhi. A fresh clone, a different machine, a different agent in the swarm (Codex, Astra, the desktop app), or this same operator talking to Pravrudhi through any surface other than this specific Claude Code session on this specific machine, has no automatic capture at all.

Even where the hook is installed, it does not capture "every" ask by its own documented design (confirmed against the operator's own prior memory note on this exact mechanism): it skips prompts under 80 characters, skips prompts containing harness markers, skips near-duplicates, and **swallows every failure silently** — so if the hook script breaks, asks stop being recorded with no signal from inside Pravrudhi that anything was missed. The memory record documents this already happened once: five substantial asks went uncaptured in one afternoon.

So the acceptance criterion's evidence is real and the cited code is solid, but it demonstrates a manual/optional ledger API plus two narrow integrations (Telegram, a watchdog) — not the property actually asked for, which was that the *engine itself* durably remembers every ask made of it. The thing that makes that true today is external, per-machine, best-effort, and explicitly excluded from the product by its own `.gitignore`. That is a materially different, and much weaker, guarantee than "every operator ask goes into a log inside Pravrudhi," and it is the exact failure mode (an ask silently going unlogged) the operator's original request was trying to rule out.

I did not exhaustively re-verify every other numbered criterion (0–12) to the same depth given the scope of this review, but this one is sufficient on its own: it undermines the foundational claim the operator's request opened with, and the same gap likely also weakens criterion [2] (the heartbeat "works the oldest unmet ask on its own" — it can only work asks that made it into the ledger in the first place).

roster.note: Costs nothing and, on the evidence so far, does little: it produced no change at all on two tasks a hosted agent completed in minutes. Serving text and driving an agentic tool-calling loop are different capabilities. Restored to the mechanical tier only, and declared behind sonnet, so it is reached solely when the paid route is cooling. Last resort, not a peer.

The same Lite Plan, its cheap high-throughput model. Added 2026-09-08 after the plan's one-week quota was exhausted inside a day. The cause was not one expensive call: qwen3.8-max, the vendor's FLAGSHIP, was the declared first choice at both mechanical and standard, driving agent loops whose steps cost about 20,000 tokens each (one measured step of a trivial task: 20,419 total, 19,584 read from cache), dispatched hourly. Mechanical work is what a fast cheap model is for. The two share one quota, so this buys no capacity; it lowers the burn rate for the work that never needed the flagship, which is most of it. Admitted at mechanical only -- the same tier the plan's other model earned on one verified tool call -- because a cheaper model is not thereby a better one.

Alibaba's Lite Plan flagship, on a plan-exclusive endpoint with its own key file and a credit budget rather than a free-tier token cap. Verified live on 2026-09-07: given a file and a read tool it called the tool and returned the right answer, exit 0 in 8.6s. Admitted at the two tiers the free-tier loop was admitted at, on the same evidence and the same reasoning -- one verified tool call says the loop runs, not that it does design or critical work well. It is declared ahead of the free-tier loop because it is cheaper and the vendor's stronger model, and it rises further only on its measured record here.

A hosted free-tier model with no CLI: it cannot drive a tool-calling loop, only answer once with a JSON payload of whole-file contents. It is the SENTINEL. Permitted at every tier but declared last everywhere above mechanical, so the router reaches it only when every paid route at that tier is cooling down from a usage limit. A single-shot writer is a poor substitute for an agent loop and a far better one than a stopped loop, which is what the operator asked for on 2026-09-06: the system must run unattended when the paid accounts are spent. It stays because the loop above it is a different route and can also be spent.

Out of the tiers since 2026-09-08: the free tier's coding quota is spent. Asked to do work it answers "The free quota has been exhausted", observed through the agent rather than assumed, so it is a route the swarm can no longer choose. The subscribed Lite Plan (qwen-lite-max) is the Alibaba seat that works and is first at both tiers it serves.
